fields.label: Hours per day
fields.help: How many hours of streaming per day.

explanation:
One hour of high-definition video streaming emits roughly **36 grams of CO₂** on a global-average grid. That figure is far lower than the widely-shared 2019 estimates (which pegged it near 3,200 g/hr) — the International Energy Agency revised the number down sharply in 2020 after correcting for how data centres and networks actually scale. Resolution is the single biggest lever you control: jumping from SD to 4K multiplies the data moved per second by roughly 7×, and emissions rise with it.

## How the calculation works

This calculator multiplies your daily hours by an emission factor that depends on resolution:

`g CO₂/day = hours/day × quality factor`, then `kg/month = g/day × 30 ÷ 1,000`.

- **SD (480p)**: ~10 g CO₂/hour
- **HD (1080p)**: ~36 g CO₂/hour
- **4K (2160p)**: ~75 g CO₂/hour

So 2 hours a day in HD works out to 72 g/day, or about **2.2 kg CO₂/month** — roughly the same as driving a petrol car 9–10 km. Most of those emissions live in the network and data centre, **not** your TV; the screen itself is a small slice unless it's a large 4K panel.

## What actually moves the needle

Three habits cut streaming emissions with no loss of experience:

- **Drop resolution on small screens.** 4K on a phone is invisible to the eye but doubles the data load versus HD. Match resolution to screen size.
- **Use WiFi over cellular.** A 4G/5G connection uses roughly 60% more energy per gigabyte than home WiFi, because the radio access network is far less efficient than a fixed line.
- **Don't leave video autoplaying.** Background autoplay and "watch next" loops on a paused screen still pull a full video stream. Turn off autoplay to stop streaming you're not watching.

The biggest variable the calculator can't see is your local grid: an hour streamed in coal-heavy Poland emits several times more than the same hour in hydro-powered Norway. Treat the result as a global-average estimate, not a regional one.

faq.q: How much CO₂ is produced per hour of streaming?
faq.a: Standard Definition (SD): ~10g/hr. High Definition (HD): ~36g/hr. 4K: ~75g/hr. Most emissions come from data center servers and network infrastructure.

faq.q: Does WiFi vs. mobile (4G/5G) make a difference?
faq.a: Yes. WiFi uses about 60% less energy than cellular networks. Always use WiFi at home when available to reduce your streaming emissions.

faq.q: Does dark mode actually reduce carbon emissions?
faq.a: On OLED displays, yes. Dark mode can reduce power consumption by ~30% because OLED pixels emit their own light. YouTube dark theme is an easy way to help.

faq.q: Is streaming from Netflix vs. YouTube different?
faq.a: Similar overall impact. Services with better video compression (often YouTube) tend to emit slightly less CO₂ per hour of viewing.

faq.q: Is it better to download than stream?
faq.a: If you'll watch more than twice, downloading saves energy. For one-time viewing, the impact is similar—download bandwidth isn't free.
These are estimates using internationally validated formulas. Actual emissions vary by region (grid carbon intensity), service, and device. For critical decisions, consult a professional.
